title: Rock Sliders for the Unibody

citations.title: Rocky Road Outfitters — ZJ armor and sliders
JCR Offroad — ZJ Grand Cherokee armor

summary: On a body-on-frame truck a crushed rocker is cosmetic. On a unibody ZJ the rocker pinch seam is part of the structure that holds the vehicle together, so protecting it is not optional once you start putting the truck on rocks. A good slider spreads trail impacts into the strongest part of the body and gives you a place to high-lift and to step.
description:
The ZJ carries its loads through the body, not a separate ladder frame. Catch the rocker on a ledge and you can tweak door gaps and crack seam sealer, which then invites the rust the ZJ is already prone to. Sliders turn that vulnerable seam into an armored rail. They also give a solid, rated lift point — the factory pinch seam is a poor place to put a jack on the trail.

Bolt-on sliders that clamp and through-bolt to the pinch seam install in an afternoon and suit a mild-trail ZJ. For hard use, weld-on or hybrid designs that tie into the floor structure carry far more load without distorting the seam. If you wheel ledges and like to slide the body across rock, spend the extra effort on a design that welds in.

Test-fit before final mounting and confirm the slider clears your tire at full stuff and does not foul the doors. Seal and paint any drilled holes to keep water out of the rocker cavity — an unprotected drilled hole on a ZJ is a rust start. Recheck the hardware after the first few trail runs.

Because the ZJ carries its loads through the body, the rocker is the one panel you cannot shrug off bending. Sliders convert that liability into an armored rail and a usable lift point. Mild builds can bolt them on; hard-use trucks should weld in. Either way, seal every drilled hole so the rocker cavity does not become a rust trap.

title: Skid Plates — Engine, Trans, and Fuel Tank

citations.title: Rocky Road Outfitters — ZJ skid plates and underbody armor
cad4x4 — ZJ winch plate with skid plate

summary: The two things under a ZJ you cannot afford to puncture are the fuel tank and the transfer case, and both sit low and unprotected from the factory. Underbody armor is the least glamorous money on a build and some of the best spent — a single dropped transfer case or holed tank ends the trip and the repair dwarfs the skid.
description:
Start with the fuel tank skid: the ZJ tank hangs behind the rear axle and takes the first hit on a steep exit. Next is the transfer case and the low-hanging crossmember, then the engine and oil pan. A trans-mounted skid also protects the exposed linkage and lines that a rock can otherwise snag.

Steel skids cost less and take repeated abuse, at the price of weight that a short, nose-heavy ZJ feels. Aluminum costs more and saves pounds where the truck wants it least — over the front axle. For a budget mild-trail build, steel is the sensible call; for a weight-conscious crawler, aluminum on the front and steel out back is a reasonable split.

Most ZJ skids bolt to existing crossmember points with minimal drilling. Use the supplied or grade-8 hardware and torque it down — a skid that vibrates loose becomes a drag anchor. After hard hits, drop the skid and check for cracks in the mounts and for fuel or fluid weeping behind it. Paint scrapes so the steel does not flash-rust.

Underbody armor is insurance against the single hit that ends a trip. Protect the fuel tank and transfer case first, then the engine and crossmember. Steel for budget builds, aluminum up front for weight-conscious crawlers. Inspect the skids and their mounts after hard hits, and touch up scrapes so bare steel does not flash-rust under the truck where you never see it.

title: Front Winch Bumper

parts.name: Front winch bumper (bolt-on or DIY weld kit)

citations.title: JCR Offroad — DIY ZJ front winch bumper (92-98)
cad4x4 — ZJ winch plate with skid plate

summary: The factory ZJ plastic fascia hangs low, blocks the approach angle, and offers nothing to recover from. A steel front bumper fixes all three at once — it trims the overhang for a steeper approach, gives the winch a structural home, and adds rated recovery points. It is one of the highest-value armor pieces on the truck.
description:
The ZJ's long front overhang and low air dam are the first things to drag on a steep climb. A trimmed steel bumper pulls the leading edge up and back for a meaningfully better approach angle, and replaces brittle plastic with something that shrugs off a rock or a brush hit. Look for integrated recovery points or shackle tabs that are welded, not bolted to thin tabs.

The JCR DIY kit ships as laser-cut steel you tack and weld together, which costs less and lets you fit it precisely — worth it if you can weld or know someone who can. A finished bolt-on bumper installs in an afternoon with hand tools for builders who would rather not fabricate. Either way the bumper should mount to the frame rails, not the crash-can stubs.

If the bumper holds your winch, the line pull goes through the bumper into the frame, so the mounting design has to be up to that. The cad4x4 winch-plate approach in the sources integrates the winch mount with a skid for exactly this reason. Confirm clearance for your tire at full lock and that the bumper does not block airflow to the radiator, which a ZJ guards jealously in heat.

A steel front bumper is three upgrades in one: better approach angle, a structural winch home, and rated recovery points. The non-negotiable is that it mounts to the frame rails and carries the winch load into structure, not into a thin bracket. Confirm tire clearance at lock and keep the radiator airflow open, and the nose of the ZJ is transformed.

title: Adding a Locker — Dana 35 and Dana 44

citations.title: Quadratec — 1993-1998 Grand Cherokee ZJ lockers
East Coast Gear Supply — Dana 35 lockers and carriers

summary: Of every dollar you can spend on a ZJ's trail capability, a rear locker returns the most climb per dollar — an open differential sends torque to the tire with the least grip, and a locker forces both rear tires to drive together. The catch is that the ZJ's rear axle dictates which locker is wise.
description:
Six-cylinder ZJs almost always have a Dana 35 rear; V8 trucks got the stronger Dana 44. The 44 takes a locker, lower gears, and 33s without complaint, so build it without hesitation. The Dana 35 is a c-clip axle that can shear a shaft when a locker plants both tires under a big tire on a hard ledge. A locked 35 on 31s driven with mechanical sympathy lives a long time; a locked 35 on 33s wheeled hard is on borrowed time. Read the axle identification guide before you buy.

A selectable air locker (ARB and the Yukon Zip are common ZJ choices per the Quadratec listing) stays fully open until you flip a switch, so street manners are unchanged — the premium option. An automatic locker like the Aussie or a Lock-Right is cheaper and needs no air line, but ratchets and clicks on tight pavement turns. A limited-slip is the mild middle ground for a daily-driven ZJ that sees light trail.

If you are pulling the carrier anyway, regear at the same time and pay the setup labor once. A selectable up front (Dana 30) is worth it on a dedicated crawler, but most ZJ builds put the locker in the rear first and leave the front open or limited-slip. Backlash and bearing preload still have to be set correctly — treat this as axle setup work, not a bolt-in.

title: Which Rear Axle You Have — and What to Do With It

citations.title: Jeep axle reference — List of Jeep axles
ZJ Dana 44 application — PartsBreakers

summary: Before you plan a single upgrade, find out which rear axle is under your ZJ — it changes everything. The 4.0L inline-six trucks got a Dana 35; the 5.2L and 5.9L V8 trucks got a Dana 44 with an aluminum center section. The 44 is the one worth building; the 35 is the one to plan around.
description:
This is a reference check, not a procedure, and it saves you from buying the wrong parts. The quick tell: a Dana 35 cover is roughly round with a slightly squared bottom; the ZJ Dana 44 cover is more clearly hexagonal and the casting says so. The factory ratio is stamped on a tag at the cover or differential, and the build sheet ties it to the engine — six-cylinder ZJs are almost always 35s, V8 ZJs almost always 44s. If you have a V8 ZJ, you own one of the better factory rear axles Jeep ever put under a Grand Cherokee.

What to do with each: the Dana 44 takes a locker, lower gears, and 33s without complaint — build it. The Dana 35, as in every Jeep that got one, is fine on 30–31s and unlocked, but it is c-clip and breaks under a locked rear on bigger tires. If you have a 35 and want to wheel hard, the cleanest path is finding a take-out V8 ZJ Dana 44 and swapping it in — same chassis, near bolt-in, and you keep the disc brakes and parking-brake setup.

Whatever you have, regear front and rear together for your tire size. The front is a Dana 30 on every ZJ; it must match the rear ratio exactly.

title: Rust Inspection and Repair — ZJ Grand Cherokee Unibody

citations.title: Grand Cherokee ZJ Forum — Rust and Unibody Repair
ZJ Grand Cherokee Technical Reference — Unibody Construction

summary: The ZJ Grand Cherokee's unibody construction means rocker panels and floor pan sections are structural members, not cosmetic sheet metal. Rust here is a safety issue, not a repair-it-later problem.
description:
On a body-on-frame vehicle like a Wrangler or truck, the frame carries the structural load — body rust is ugly but rarely dangerous. The ZJ unibody works differently: the rocker panels, floor pan, and front frame horns are all load-bearing members of the structure. A badly rusted rocker panel compromises door alignment, reduces crash protection, and can cause the vehicle to flex dangerously on uneven terrain. A rotted floor pan weakens the torsional rigidity the entire suspension system depends on.

Northern-state ZJs are notorious for this. The wheel wells, inner rockers, and floor pan collect salt and moisture for years before the damage becomes visible from outside. Many ZJs that look acceptable from a car-wash distance have rocker panels that are mostly air underneath the paint. Do not assume cosmetic condition reflects structural condition.

Conduct the inspection with the vehicle on jack stands, good lighting underneath, and a sharp flathead screwdriver. Work through these areas in order:

**Rocker panels:** Poke the screwdriver into the outer rocker panel skin every few inches along its length. Sound metal resists; rusted metal collapses or punches through with little force. Pull back the carpet inside the cab and inspect the rocker panel from inside — this is where the inner rocker meets the floor pan. Probe the seam. Any softness here is structural rust.

**Floor pan:** Remove the floor mats entirely. Look for bubbling paint, soft spots, or actual holes. Poke the pan under the driver and passenger feet, under the rear seat, and along the transmission tunnel edges. Surface rust that has not perforated the metal is acceptable. Holes or paper-thin sections are not.

**Front frame horns:** These are the forward extensions of the unibody that mount the bumper and recovery hardware. Get under the vehicle and probe the frame horn surfaces. A tow hook or winch bumper mounts here — if these are rusted through, those mounts are not trustworthy and a recovery pull could tear them out entirely.

**Spare tire well:** The recessed spare tire area in the cargo floor is a rust trap. It collects water that sits against the pan. Check the perimeter of the well where it meets the cargo floor.

Surface rust — discoloration, light pitting, or flaking without perforation — is normal on a 25–30 year old vehicle and treatable with rust converter and paint. This is not a safety issue.

Perforated metal or sections that collapse under screwdriver pressure are structural failures. Assess the extent: a 3" hole in the outer rocker skin with solid inner rocker behind it is repairable. A rocker that is completely hollow — both inner and outer skins gone — for more than 12" of its length is a major structural repair that requires significant fabrication skill and cost.

The honest assessment: a ZJ with severe floor pan rot across more than half the driver or passenger footwell, or with rocker panels missing both skins for most of their length, may cost more to repair correctly than the vehicle is worth. A qualified rust repair shop can quote the job — get that quote before investing in any other modifications.

**Minor rust (surface to small perforations under 3"):** Grind to bare metal, treat with Ospho or POR-15 rust converter, allow to cure, apply weld-through primer, weld in patch panel or use metal-reinforced epoxy for truly minor surface repairs. Coat the finished repair inside and out with Eastwood frame coating or rubberized undercoat.

**Rocker panel replacement:** This is the most common ZJ rust repair. Obtain patch panels from Raybuck or equivalent. Cut back to solid metal — do not stop at the rust line, cut another inch or two past it into good steel. Weld in the patch with 1" stitch welds to control heat distortion. Prime and coat immediately; bare metal on a ZJ rusts fast.

**Floor pan sections:** Remove the carpet and sound deadening. Cut out perforated areas with an angle grinder. Fit and weld in patch panels. Apply seam sealer to all welds inside the cab. Re-coat the underside with rubberized undercoating. Replace the sound deadening — it holds moisture if left wet.

**Internal rocker treatment:** Before closing up any rocker panel work, spray the internal cavity with Eastwood Internal Frame Coating or a cavity wax such as Fluid Film. These penetrate and displace moisture. Do this annually on any ZJ you plan to keep — the rockers are hollow and collect condensation even in dry climates over time.

title: Front Brake Pad and Rotor Replacement
tools_required: 11mm or 13mm wrench (caliper bracket bolts — varies by year)

parts.name: Front brake pads (semi-metallic)
parts.part_number: Wagner ZD436 / Bosch BC436 / Akebono ACT436

parts.name: Brake cleaner (aerosol, non-chlorinated)
parts.vendor: CRC, Berryman, any auto parts store

citations.title: Cherokeeforum ZJ front brake replacement how-to
ZJ service info

summary: Front pads on the ZJ wear faster than the rears because the system is biased forward. Plan on 2 hours for both sides if it's your first time, 45 minutes once you've done it. Always replace pads in axle pairs — never one side.
description:
The ZJ uses a single-piston floating caliper up front, the same basic design as the XJ Cherokee and TJ Wrangler. Pads run $25–$45 a set; rotors $60–$100 a pair. Don't cheap out on rotors — the bottom-tier $25/rotor specials warp within a year in Phoenix heat or any city driving with frequent hard stops. Centric or Bosch coated rotors hold up.

Wagner ZD436, Bosch BC436, and Akebono ACT436 are all solid pad choices. Avoid the lowest-tier organic pads on a ZJ — the rotors are heavy enough that organic pads glaze quickly and start squealing within 5,000 miles. Semi-metallic is the right pad family for a 4,000-lb SUV that gets driven hard.

Before you start: pump the brake pedal a few times with the engine off to bleed pressure off the system, crack the master cylinder cap (helps the caliper piston retract without forcing fluid backward), and have a friend or some shop towels nearby because new-pad break-in always involves a couple of "interesting" stops.
steps: Loosen the front lug nuts a quarter turn with the wheels on the ground, then jack and support the vehicle on jack stands. Never work under a vehicle held up only by a jack.
Remove the wheels. Inspect the caliper, slide pins, and dust boots for tears.
Crack the master cylinder cap (don't remove it fully — break the seal so fluid can move).
Push the caliper piston back into the bore. A large C-clamp against an old pad face works; a piston-retraction tool is faster.
Remove the two caliper guide bolts (13mm) and lift the caliper up and off. Hang it from the upper control arm with a bungee or coat hanger — never let it hang by the brake hose.
Slide the old pads out. Note the inboard pad has the wear-indicator clip on the inside.
Remove the two caliper bracket bolts (typically 11mm or 13mm hex, varies by year — some are an external E-Torx) and lift the bracket off.
Pull the old rotor straight off the hub. If it's stuck, give it a few sharp hits with a dead-blow hammer on the hat (not the friction surface).
Spray brake cleaner on the new rotor to remove the shipping oil. Slide the new rotor onto the hub.
Reinstall the caliper bracket. Torque the bracket bolts to 70 ft-lbs (verify in a 1993–1998 ZJ service manual for your year — some years spec higher).
Apply a thin film of silicone brake grease to the slide pin contact surfaces and the back of each pad where it touches the caliper.
Slide the new pads into the bracket. Lower the caliper over the pads.
Reinstall the two caliper guide bolts. Torque to 25–30 ft-lbs (per the FSM).
Reinstall the wheel. Torque lug nuts to 90 ft-lbs in a star pattern.

With the wheel back on, sit in the driver's seat and pump the brake pedal until it firms up — usually 3–5 pumps. **This step is mandatory.** Driving without pumping the pedal first means no brakes on the first stop.
Check the master cylinder level; top off with DOT 3.

Bed in the new pads: 6 to 8 firm stops from 30 mph to 5 mph, then 30 minutes of normal driving without sitting on the brake at a long stoplight (the pad material smears onto the rotor and creates the friction surface — sitting still while it's hot causes pad imprinting).
pros: Direct, well-documented job — no special tools required
One of the few brake jobs where DIY savings (~$200 over a shop) actually justify the time
A fresh front brake setup makes the ZJ feel like a different vehicle if the old pads were glazed
cons: Front pads wear roughly twice as fast as rears on the ZJ — plan on replacement every 30,000 to 50,000 miles in city driving
Cheap rotors will warp; the savings aren't worth it
Pumping the brake pedal before driving is non-negotiable — skip that step and the first stop is empty pedal to the floor

title: Coolant Flush — 4.0 and Magnum V8

parts.name: Mopar 5-year/100K extended-life antifreeze (OAT), 1 gal
parts.vendor: any auto parts store; Prestone Cor-Guard or equivalent is fine

citations.title: ZJ 4.0L coolant capacity (Haynes reference)
ZJ service info — cooling system

summary: The ZJ 4.0L cooling system holds about 12.7 quarts; the Magnum V8s hold about 14 quarts. Plan on flushing with distilled water twice, then refilling with a 50/50 mix of distilled water and extended-life antifreeze. Bleed the air through the bleed plug on the thermostat housing — skip that step and you'll overheat within 10 miles.
description:
A ZJ that's never had a coolant flush will run hot in Phoenix summer, especially with the AC on, and the heater core will weep onto the passenger floor mat before it finally gives up. The 4.0L straight-six and the Magnum V8s both share an aluminum radiator on a plastic tank — these tanks crack with age, and old acidic coolant accelerates the failure. Flushing every 50,000 miles is the cheapest insurance you can buy against a $250 radiator.

The original Mopar HOAT (red) coolant was good for 5 years or 100,000 miles. Modern Mopar extended-life OAT coolant is fully backward-compatible with the ZJ if the system is fully flushed first. Don't mix coolant chemistries — flush twice with distilled water until what comes out is clear, then refill with a single coolant type. Prestone Cor-Guard, Peak Long Life, and Mopar's current OAT spec all work.

The radiator drain is a plastic petcock on the passenger-side bottom of the radiator. Most are old, brittle, and snap off when you turn them with pliers. Have a $25 replacement petcock on hand before you start. The block drain is a 1/4" NPT plug on the driver's side of the block — pull that too if you want a full flush, but it's optional and clears most of the residual coolant.
steps: Run the engine until it's at full operating temperature, then shut down and let it cool for at least an hour. Hot coolant under pressure scalds — wait until the cap is cool to the touch.
Remove the radiator cap. Position a drain pan under the radiator petcock (passenger-side bottom).
Open the radiator petcock — twist counterclockwise, gently. If it cracks, replace with a new petcock before continuing.
Drain into the pan, then transfer to a 5-gallon bucket. Old coolant is hazardous waste — take it to an AutoZone or O'Reilly for free recycling.
Close the petcock, fill the radiator with distilled water. Run the engine with the heater on full hot for 10 minutes to circulate.
Shut down, let cool, drain. Repeat until what drains is clear — usually two cycles is enough.
Close the petcock for the last time. Refill with a 50/50 mix of distilled water and OAT coolant. The 4.0L needs about 6 quarts of each; the V8s need about 7 of each.
Open the bleed plug on the thermostat housing (top of engine, on the upper radiator hose inlet). Fill until coolant runs out of the bleed hole air-free. Close the bleed plug.
Top off the radiator. Leave the cap off, run the engine with the heater on full hot for 15 minutes, watching the temp gauge. Top off as the coolant level drops.
Install the cap, run it up to operating temp, drive a few miles. Re-check level the next day — overflow bottle should be between MIN and MAX cold.
pros: Cheap maintenance — $25 in supplies, no special tools
The single biggest predictor of long-term cooling system reliability
Catches a failing radiator or weeping water pump before they leave you stuck
cons: The plastic radiator petcock breaks more often than not on a ZJ that's never been serviced — have a spare on hand
Air pockets in the heater core will cause overheating even after a "good" flush — bleed the system properly or repeat the bleed procedure after the first drive
The old MEG (green) coolant must be fully flushed before refilling with OAT — mixing causes gelling and ruins the water pump

title: Re-gear for Bigger Tires

parts.name: Ring and pinion set, front + rear (4.56 or 4.11)

citations.title: East Coast Gear Supply — Jeep Dana 35 gears and install kits
Iron Rock Off Road — ZJ 93-98 build parts

summary: Going from factory 30-inch tires to 31s or 33s without re-gearing leaves the ZJ chronically under-geared: the engine labors, the automatic shifts late and overheats, and highway mileage drops. Re-gearing both differentials is the fix that makes a lifted ZJ drivable again, and on a build with 33s it is mandatory, not optional.
description:
Factory ZJ ratios run roughly 3.55 (V8) to 3.73 (some 4.0L). On 31s a move to 3.73 or 4.10 is enough; on 33s most builders land on 4.56, and the search results above show that as the common recommendation. Run the numbers for your tire diameter and transmission, then gear both axles to the same ratio — mismatched front and rear ratios bind the transfer case on the street.

The ZJ is full-time or selectable four-wheel drive depending on transfer case, and the front and rear must spin at the same effective speed. Re-gear one axle only and you create a ratio mismatch that loads the drivetrain and chews the transfer case chain. Do front and rear in one job and you also avoid paying the setup labor twice.

Ring-and-pinion setup is the most precision-dependent work in the database — pinion depth, backlash, and bearing preload all have to land inside tight tolerances or the gears howl and fail. If you have not set up a third member before, this is the job to hand to a shop. Buy quality gears and a master install kit per axle, and keep the Dana 35 rear honest about its limits: lower gears plus a locker plus 33s is the load that breaks the c-clip 35, so read the axle guide before you commit.

title: Transfer Case Guide — NP231, NV242, NV249 in the ZJ

parts.name: JB Conversions SYE kit for NP231
Tom Wood's CV rear driveshaft (ZJ NP231 SYE)

citations.title: ZJ Grand Cherokee Transfer Case Identification — Novak Conversions
NP231 SYE Installation — JeepForum ZJ

summary: The ZJ uses one of three transfer cases depending on trim and model year. Know which one you have before lifting the vehicle — the SYE requirement above 4" of lift applies to the NP231 specifically, and the NV249 has a known chain wear issue at high mileage.
description:
Three transfer cases appear in the ZJ depending on the drive system selected at the factory. The **NP231** (also called the Command-Trac) is the part-time unit found in base Sport and Country trims — it runs in 2H for normal driving and requires shifting into 4H or 4L manually. This is the most common and the most upgradeable.

The **NV242** (SelectTrac) is a combination part-time/full-time unit. It adds a neutral-4WD position and a full-time 4H mode that distributes torque front and rear continuously. The NV242 is robust and relatively simple internally.

The **NV249** (Quadra-Trac II) is the full-time unit found on higher-trim ZJs. It uses a planetary differential center section that allows variable torque split. The NV249 cannot be operated in true 2WD — it is always in some form of 4WD. This is fine for street use but costs fuel economy and creates minor driveline bind in some road conditions.

To identify which unit you have: the NP231 has a circular shifter pattern with 2H-N-4H-4L. The NV242 adds a 4WD Full position. The NV249 has an electronic push-button selector (no floor shifter in some models) and no 2H position.

This is the most important piece of information for anyone lifting a ZJ with an NP231 or NV242 past 4 inches. Both units use a slip yoke on the rear output — the rear driveshaft slides onto the output shaft and relies on slip to handle the length change as the suspension cycles. At stock ride height, the driveline angle is within spec. Raise the vehicle 4" or more and the driveshaft angle becomes extreme, causing vibration at highway speed and accelerated U-joint wear.

A Slip Yoke Eliminator (SYE) replaces the slip yoke with a flanged output, converting to a double-cardan (CV) rear driveshaft. The CV joint absorbs the angle change that the slip yoke previously handled. BYP Manufacturing and JB Conversions both make NP231 SYE kits that are well-regarded in the ZJ community — either kit runs around $285–295. After installing the SYE, the stock rear driveshaft will not work; a new CV driveshaft from Tom Wood's or Adams Driveshafts is required (figure $280–310 for a custom-measured unit).

This is not an optional upgrade at 4" of lift. The vibration from an un-SYE'd NP231 at 4" is significant and the U-joints will fail prematurely. Budget for SYE + driveshaft as part of any serious lift.

The NV249's planetary center section sits in front of a drive chain that transfers power to the rear output shaft. On high-mileage units (above 120,000 miles), the chain stretches and begins to slap against the housing. The symptom is a distinct clattering or rattling noise under light throttle or deceleration in 4WD, sometimes audible in 2WD mode as well. Novak Conversions and other suppliers sell NV249 chain replacement kits ($175–190) — replacing the chain requires removing the transfer case and disassembling the unit. It is not a field repair. If you are buying a high-mileage ZJ with the NV249, ask specifically about chain noise; a slapping NV249 chain is a repair cost to factor into the purchase price.

The NP231, NV242, and NV249 all take ATF+4 fluid. The factory service interval is 30,000 miles under normal use; 15,000 miles if the vehicle sees regular water crossings or off-road use. Drain and fill capacity is roughly 1 quart for the NP231 and NV242, and about 1.5 quarts for the NV249. Use Mopar ATF+4 or a compatible equivalent — do not use ATF Dex/Merc in these units.

title: Auxiliary Lighting Done Right

citations.title: Rocky Road Outfitters — ZJ accessories and lighting mounts
Iron Rock Off Road — ZJ 93-98 products

summary: The factory ZJ headlights were never strong and decades of hazing have made them worse, so aux lighting is one of the cheaper upgrades that genuinely improves how the truck wheels after dark. The wiring is where people go wrong: power any real lighting load through a relay and a fuse, not through a dash switch carrying the full current.
description:
Match the optic to the job. A wide flood or diffused pattern lights the immediate trail and is best for slow crawling where you want to see the lines beside you. A spot or driving pattern throws far down a graded road. A common ZJ setup is a pair of ditch or A-pillar pods on flood for the trail plus a bar or driving pair for distance, each on its own switch.

Run a proper harness: power from the battery through a fuse to a relay, the relay triggered by a low-current dash switch, and the switched output to the lights. This keeps heavy current out of the cabin and protects the circuit if a wire chafes through on the trail. Ground to clean bare metal, not a painted or rusty ZJ body panel, or the lights will flicker.

Mount pods to the bumper, A-pillars, or a roof rack with vibration in mind — a light that rattles loose on washboard is worse than no light. Aim them on a wall before the first night run so you are not blinding yourself off the hood. Keep the highest-mounted bar legal and covered for street use; an uncovered bar on the road draws tickets and glare complaints.

Aux lighting is among the cheapest upgrades that genuinely improves night wheeling on a ZJ, but only when it is wired correctly. Power the lights through a fused relay triggered by a low-current switch, ground to bare metal, and aim them before the first night run. Match the beam pattern to whether you crawl slow or cover graded road fast.

title: Dual Battery and Charging Upgrade

citations.title: Rocky Road Outfitters — ZJ electrical and accessory mounts
Grand Cherokee ZJ build references — Expedition Portal

summary: The moment a ZJ build adds a winch, recovery lighting, or an overland fridge, the lone factory battery stops being enough — a long winch pull or a night parked running a fridge can leave you with a truck that will not crank. A dual-battery system separates the loads that must never drain your start battery from everything else.
description:
The point is isolation. The starting battery stays dedicated to firing the engine; the auxiliary battery carries the winch, the fridge, the lights, and any camp loads. A voltage-sensitive relay or a DC-DC charger ties them together only when the alternator is charging, so you can flatten the aux battery overnight and still start in the morning. A DC-DC unit also charges an AGM or lithium aux battery correctly, which a voltage-only relay does not.

Match the aux battery to the loads. A deep-cycle AGM tolerates the repeated discharge of camp use far better than a plain starting battery, and seals against the vibration and angles a ZJ sees on the trail. If you are running a winch hard, a high-output aux battery and heavy interconnect cable keep voltage from sagging mid-pull.

A built ZJ that adds a winch and a fridge can outrun the factory alternator, so consider a higher-output unit if the voltage drops under load. Fuse every run close to its battery, use cable sized for the current, and mount the second battery where heat and water stay out — the ZJ engine bay is tight, so many builders relocate the aux battery to the cargo area with proper venting and a sealed box.

Once a ZJ runs a winch and a fridge, isolation is what keeps you from a no-start morning. Dedicate the main battery to starting, carry accessory loads on a deep-cycle aux battery, and tie them with a smart isolator or DC-DC charger. Size the cable to the current, fuse close to each battery, and vent the aux box if you relocate it to the cargo area.

title: 4.0L Straight-Six Engine — ZJ Overview, Common Issues, and Upgrades

citations.title: Jeep 4.0L Engine Technical Guide — Allpar.com
ZJ Crankshaft Position Sensor Diagnosis — JeepForum

summary: The ZJ's 4.0L straight-six is the same essential engine used in the XJ Cherokee, TJ Wrangler, and WJ Grand Cherokee — one of Jeep's most durable powerplants. Know its failure points and it will run for 250,000+ miles.
description:
The 4.0L High Output inline-six produces 190–195 hp and 225 lb-ft of torque in ZJ specification. Those numbers are modest, but the 4.0L's power band is wide and low — it pulls hard from 1,500 RPM, which is exactly what you want on a technical trail. The engine is also physically robust: cast iron block, seven main bearings, and an interference-free valvetrain. Oil pressure and temperature will be on your side if you maintain the cooling system.

The 1993–1995 ZJ uses the OBD1 version; the 1996–1998 ZJ transitions to OBD2. The OBD2 version (1996–1998) added a second oxygen sensor and refined fueling — it runs cleaner but is mechanically the same. Both versions respond to the same service procedures.

The crankshaft position sensor (CPS) is the most common failure point on the 4.0L ZJ, particularly on 1993–1999 vehicles. The sensor reads the crank reluctor ring and triggers the ignition and fuel injection. When it fails, the symptoms are dramatic: no-start, stalling at operating temperature, or intermittent stalling that gets worse as the engine warms up. The sensor is mounted on the bell housing facing the flywheel — it sits in an area that gets heat-soaked on a warm engine. Heat expansion causes an intermittent open circuit in the sensor windings.

The fix is a replacement CPS from Mopar or Standard Motor Products (BWD or Intermotor brand). Avoid no-name sensors — quality matters here, as a bad replacement will leave you stranded just like the original. The replacement takes about 45 minutes; there are two bolts, a connector, and the need to properly set the sensor gap to the flywheel (typically 0.030"–0.050"). Code P0340 or P0344 on OBD2 (or equivalent flash codes on OBD1) points directly to this sensor.

The 4.0L's intake manifold includes a plastic coolant crossover pipe that bridges the front and rear of the manifold. On older ZJs, this pipe cracks at its plastic joints or at the manifold interface, leading to coolant loss. The failure mode is often slow — a small seep that gets worse over time. Symptoms include a coolant smell from the engine bay with no visible external leak, or a gradual drop in coolant level without overheating (until it gets bad).

The replacement pipe is a Mopar part. The repair involves draining the cooling system, removing the intake manifold, and replacing the crossover pipe. Some owners replace the plastic crossover with an aluminum unit as an upgrade; the Dorman aluminum crossover ($55–70) is a common choice and eliminates the plastic failure mode entirely.

The 4.0L head gasket is not a routine failure item unless the engine has been overheated. A ZJ that overheated — low coolant, stuck thermostat, failed water pump — may have a compromised head gasket. Signs include white exhaust smoke, coolant loss without visible external leak, bubbles in the overflow reservoir, or a sweet smell from the exhaust. A cold start pressure test of the cooling system and a combustion leak test (using a chemical test kit) are the right diagnostic tools. If you are buying a ZJ, check the coolant for discoloration and the oil dipstick for any milkiness.

The 4.0L is not a performance engine and trying to make it one is a poor use of money. The useful upgrades are reliability and response improvements. A K&N drop-in filter ($55) is a one-time install that improves airflow slightly and never needs replacement. Upgrading to NGK Iridium plugs and quality plug wires (Accel or MSD) improves ignition reliability and cold-start performance. An MSD 6A ignition box ($185) improves spark energy and eliminates the occasional weak-spark misfire under load — worthwhile for a trail rig that idles hard and runs at low RPM on rocks.

A performance intake manifold or headers are available from Hedman and others, but the power gains are marginal and the cost high. Spend that money on suspension or axle work instead.

title: 5.2L and 5.9L Magnum V8 — ZJ Overview and Service

citations.title: Jeep 5.2L and 5.9L Magnum V8 — Allpar Technical
ZJ V8 Grand Cherokee Forum

summary: The V8 ZJ is a different animal from the 4.0L — more power, more towing capability, a stronger rear axle, and more involved service. If you are shopping for a build rig, a V8 ZJ with a solid drivetrain is worth the premium over an I6.
description:
The 5.2L Magnum V8 produces 220 hp and 300 lb-ft of torque — a significant step up from the 4.0L's 195 hp and 225 lb-ft. More importantly, the V8 ZJ comes from the factory with a stronger drivetrain: the 46RH (or 46RE with electronic shift on later models) 4-speed automatic replaces the AW4 used behind the I6, and the rear axle is a Dana 44a on V8 models rather than the Chrysler 8.25 found behind the I6. The D44a is a significantly stronger axle with better aftermarket locker and gear support.

The 5.9L Limited (1998 model year only) is rare and historically valuable in the ZJ community. It produces 245 hp and 345 lb-ft of torque — genuinely strong for the era. These trucks were loaded (genuine leather, unique badging, specific wheels) and command a premium on the used market. A clean 5.9L Limited is a collector piece and a legitimate trail rig simultaneously.

The 5.2L Magnum's intake manifold gaskets are a known failure point. The factory composite gaskets degrade over time and can leak coolant into the lifter valley or allow an intake vacuum leak. Symptoms include a small coolant loss over time, occasional rough idle, or — in a worst case — coolant in the oil if the leak routes internally. This is not as severe as a head gasket failure; it is a known service item on the 5.2L that should be addressed on any high-mileage engine.

Fel-Pro replacement gaskets are the standard repair. The job requires removing the intake manifold, cleaning all mating surfaces thoroughly, and reinstalling with fresh gaskets torqued to spec. With the engine accessible in the ZJ's relatively roomy engine bay, this is a half-day job for a competent mechanic.

The V8 ZJ's spark plug replacement is more involved than the I6 simply due to the number of cylinders (8 vs. 6) and plug location in the valley of the V configuration. The rear plugs on the driver's side are the most difficult to access. Champion RC12YC or equivalent plugs are the factory spec. Use anti-seize on plug threads — these engines are cast iron and plugs can seize over time. Replace the ignition wires at the same time; MSD 8mm wires significantly improve spark energy on the V8 and are worth the cost on a trail vehicle that runs at low RPM for extended periods.

The honest trade-off: the V8 ZJ returns 12–15 mpg in typical mixed use, versus 15–18 for the 4.0L. On a long overland trip or frequent trail days, that gap adds up. The V8 also requires premium-quality oil changes on time — the 5.2L responds poorly to extended drain intervals. Budget for higher fuel and consumable costs if you are comparing V8 to I6.

The 46RH/46RE transmission also has a different service schedule than the AW4. It requires clean ATF+4 and a clean filter; neglected examples shift harshly. A transmission service (fluid and filter, not a full flush) every 30,000 miles keeps these transmissions healthy.

The V8 ZJ's standard Dana 44a rear axle is the primary reason to seek one out as a build vehicle. The D44a uses the same basic carrier as the standard D44 used in many Jeeps — aftermarket lockers, gears, and axle shafts are well-supported. An ARB Air Locker or Powertrax Lock-Right fits the D44a directly. A ZJ with a V8 and a D44a rear, a solid D30 front, and a 46RH automatic is a better starting point for a serious moderate trail or rock crawler build than the I6 with its C8.25 rear. The powertrain premium is real, but so is the capability ceiling.

title: Fuel Pump Replacement — ZJ 4.0L and V8

citations.title: ZJ Fuel Pump Replacement Procedure — JeepForum.com
Jeep ZJ Grand Cherokee Service Manual — Fuel System

summary: The ZJ's in-tank fuel pump is a wear item that fails predictably at high mileage — hard starting when the tank is below a quarter, stalling under load, and loss of power climbing grades are the signatures. Replace it with an OEM-quality unit; bargain pumps fail quickly in older fuel systems.
description:
Before replacing the pump, confirm the diagnosis. The symptoms above — hard start on a low tank, stalling under load, power loss on grades — can also be caused by a clogged fuel filter or a failing crankshaft position sensor. Start with the cheapest checks first.

Fuel pressure is the definitive test. The ZJ 4.0L specification is **49 psi** at key-on (before engine start) and 45–49 psi at idle with the vacuum line disconnected from the fuel pressure regulator. The V8 spec is similar — 49–50 psi. Connect a fuel pressure gauge to the Schrader valve on the fuel rail (4.0L) or test port (V8). Turn the key to ON without cranking. The pump should pressurize the system within 2–3 seconds and hold 49 psi. A pump reading below 40 psi, or that takes more than 5 seconds to reach pressure, is failing.

If pressure is low, check the fuel filter before condemning the pump. The ZJ's in-line fuel filter (located on the frame rail under the vehicle) can restrict flow on high-mileage vehicles with neglected service history. Replace the filter ($18) and recheck pressure. If pressure is still low with a fresh filter, the pump is the cause.

This is not the place to buy the cheapest part on the shelf. The ZJ's fuel tank has likely accumulated sediment and varnish deposits over 25–30 years. A weak or poorly-built pump will have a short life in that environment. Delphi and Motorcraft are the OEM-equivalent quality brands for ZJ fuel pumps — they use better brushes, more robust impellers, and tighter fuel pressure regulation than no-name alternatives. Expect $195–220 for a quality module; budget pumps run $80–100 and commonly fail within a year.

The ZJ fuel pump is a complete module — pump, sender, strainer, and pressure regulator in one assembly. Do not attempt to replace just the pump element inside the module; replace the complete unit.

The ZJ's fuel pump is accessed by partially dropping the fuel tank — you do not need to fully remove it to reach the lock ring on top of the tank.

Depressurize the fuel system by removing the fuel pump fuse (or relay) and cranking the engine until it stalls. Then proceed:

1. Disconnect the negative battery cable.
2. Remove as much fuel from the tank as possible — this reduces the weight you're managing under the vehicle. Siphon from the filler neck or, on the trail, run the tank as low as practical before the job.
3. Support the tank with a floor jack and a piece of wood to distribute the load.
4. Disconnect the fuel lines (fuel line disconnect tools prevent line damage — do not use pliers).
5. Disconnect the electrical connectors and the vent lines from the top of the pump module.
6. Lower the tank 6–10 inches to access the lock ring on top.
7. Use the lock ring tool to turn the ring counterclockwise and remove the module.
8. Note the orientation of the fuel pickup tube relative to the tank — the new module must be installed at the same angle.
9. Install the new module, tighten the lock ring to 40 ft-lbs, reconnect everything, and raise the tank.

After reinstalling, turn the key to ON three times without cranking to prime the system, then start the engine. Check all connections for leaks. Verify fuel pressure before calling the job complete.

title: Seat Upgrades for the ZJ Grand Cherokee

citations.title: ZJ Seat Swap and Bracket Guide — JeepForum

summary: The ZJ's factory seat situation depends entirely on trim level — the Limited's leather buckets hold up reasonably well, but the Sport and Laredo cloth seats age poorly and provide limited lateral support on the trail.
description:
The ZJ Limited came with genuine leather seating that, if not cracked and dried out from UV exposure, remains comfortable and serviceable. If you have a Limited with leather seats that are in reasonable shape, there is no compelling reason to replace them unless you want more bolstering for trail use.

The Sport and Laredo trim levels used cloth seats that tend to sag, tear at the seam lines, and wear through at the bolster areas after 25+ years. More practically, neither seat provides meaningful lateral support when the vehicle is tilted on a trail — you end up bracing yourself against the door. A decent aftermarket bucket seat is a genuine quality-of-life upgrade on a trail build.

The ZJ does not have a robust aftermarket mounting bracket ecosystem the way a Wrangler does. The factory seat tracks bolt to the floor pan, and the seat mounts to those tracks. For an aftermarket seat you have two options: use the original factory tracks with an adapter plate, or replace the tracks entirely with aftermarket seat rails.

ProTrucks makes ZJ-specific bracket sets that adapt common aftermarket seats to the factory floor track mounting points. These are the cleanest solution — they maintain the fore-aft adjustment travel and correct the seat height. Universal rails from Corbeau or Sparco work as well but require drilling and measuring to ensure correct height and angle.

Seat height matters in the ZJ — the roofline is low enough that a high-back racing seat can contact the headliner or limit visibility. The Corbeau LG1 is a good choice because it is a relatively low-profile reclining bucket that fits within the ZJ cab without modification.

The **Corbeau LG1** ($280) is the practical choice for a trail-use ZJ. It is a full reclining bucket with significant side bolstering, a low enough profile for the ZJ's cab, and it accepts most standard harness configurations. It is not a racing seat — you can still get in and out normally, and it works with the factory lap/shoulder belt.

For a more committed overland or trail build, the **Corbeau A4** ($340) adds more aggressive bolstering and a fixed back — better for holding you in place on a sidehill but less convenient for daily driving. If the ZJ is a dedicated trail rig with rare street use, this is the better call.

The rear seat can be left stock or removed entirely for cargo space. The factory rear seat bottom and back release and remove with minimal effort. Removing the rear seat is a common choice on dedicated trail rigs where the extra cargo floor space is more valuable than rear passenger accommodation.

title: Cargo Management and Storage for the ZJ Grand Cherokee

parts.name: ARB roller drawer (universal, cut to fit)
Yakima LoadWarrior roof rack (ZJ roof rails)

citations.title: ZJ Overland Build — Cargo and Storage Options

summary: The ZJ has a surprisingly large cargo area for its era — competitive with many mid-size SUVs from a decade later. With the rear seat removed, the flat floor and generous width make it an effective overland platform.
description:
The ZJ cargo area measures approximately 36" wide, 44" long (with the rear seat folded or removed), and 28" in usable height. The floor is not perfectly flat with the seat folded — there is a lip at the rear seat base — but with the seat removed, the floor is close to flat from the tailgate to the back of the front seats. This is the most useful configuration for an overland build.

Aftermarket drawer systems designed for mid-size SUVs can be adapted to the ZJ with some trimming. The ARB roller drawer system is the benchmark — it provides a full-width sliding drawer with a flat top surface you can sleep on or use as a work surface, and the drawer itself stores recovery gear, tools, and camping equipment. Budget for some fabrication time to fit it correctly in the ZJ's specific floor dimensions.

A simpler approach: Pelican or MOLLE-panel systems mounted to the cargo sidewalls organize gear without the expense of a full drawer kit. L-track extrusion bolted to the cargo floor lets you strap down Pelican cases, coolers, and fuel cans without them shifting on the trail.

The ZJ has factory roof rails — the longitudinal rails running front to back on the roof. These rails are not rated for heavy loads but accept standard cross-bar feet from Yakima and Thule. The Yakima LoadWarrior or Thule Canyon XT basket mounts to these rails using the appropriate fit kit for the ZJ.

The factory roof rail system supports approximately 165 lbs static load — adequate for a lightweight tent, recovery boards, or a spare wheel (if kept under 50 lbs). Do not overload the factory rails with a full RTT (roof-top tent) unless you reinforce the rail mounting points. A roof-top tent on factory ZJ rails is a stress fracture risk over time on rough roads.

For a dedicated roof rack with higher load ratings, aftermarket full-roof racks from Wild Boar or Rhino Rack can be bolted directly to the roof with reinforcement brackets through the headliner. This is a more invasive install but allows 300+ lb loads. Measure your garage clearance before ordering — a ZJ with a full roof rack and gear on top adds 10–14" of height.

The ZJ's rear wheel wells intrude into the cargo area on both sides. These can be turned into usable storage by building or buying a wheel well box — typically a simple plywood or aluminum box that sits over the wheel arch and creates a flat surface. This adds useful cubby storage on each side without requiring the rear seat to be removed.

Keep loose gear controlled with cargo nets or rubber anti-slip matting under the flat storage area. A shifting cooler or fuel jug is a trail hazard as much as an inconvenience.

title: 42RE / 46RE Transmission Fluid Service
tools_required: drain pan (wide, low profile, 8+ qt capacity)
fluid pump or long-neck funnel (fill is through the dipstick tube)
skills_required: RTV bead control if reusing pan with no gasket
checking ATF level on a warm running transmission

parts.name: ATF+4 (5–6 quarts for filter+fluid drop, 10–12 for full flush)
parts.part_number: Mopar 05013457AA / Valvoline MaxLife ATF+4 / Castrol Transmax ATF+4

parts.name: Transmission filter and pan gasket kit (42RE)
Transmission filter and pan gasket kit (46RE V8)

citations.title: ExtremeTerrain — ZJ Service Information
JeepForum — 42RE fluid capacity discussion

summary: The 42RE (behind the 4.0L six) and the 46RE (behind the 5.2 and 5.9 Magnum V8s) are both updates to the old A500 / A518 series. They need ATF+4 — not Dexron, not Mercon, not "universal." A pan drop and filter swap takes 5 quarts and buys you 30,000 more miles of clutch life.
description:
ATF+4 is mandatory. The older ATF+3 (and the original ATF+) are superseded by ATF+4, and Mopar 05013457AA is the genuine fluid. Any ATF+4 that meets MS-9602 spec is acceptable — Valvoline MaxLife ATF+4 and Castrol Transmax both qualify. Do not run Dexron or Mercon. The frictional properties are wrong and you'll get shudder, late shifts, and eventual band damage.

A pan drop (the only practical home service — these transmissions have no drain plug) refreshes about 30% of the total fluid. Total capacity is 8.5–11 quarts dry; a service refill is 4.5–5 quarts. Plan to do a pan drop every 30,000 miles. If the fluid is burnt-smelling or dark brown instead of red, drop the pan, change the filter, and refill — then repeat the pan drop in 1,000 miles to swap more of the converter's fluid by dilution.

Service interval: 30,000 miles for normal driving. 15,000 for trail use or towing. If the previous owner never serviced it and you bought the ZJ used, do the service immediately — but if the fluid is already burnt-black, talk to a transmission shop before you do anything; a fresh-fluid shock can flush varnish loose and clog passages on a worn 42RE.
steps: Drive 15 minutes to warm the fluid. Warm ATF flows out cleanly and gives you the correct dipstick reading when you refill.
Park on a level surface and chock the front wheels. Set the parking brake firmly.
Jack the front of the vehicle and support it on jack stands. The transmission pan needs ground clearance for a drain pan underneath.

Slide the wide drain pan under the transmission pan. Loosen pan bolts (10mm or 13mm depending on year) from one corner first, working diagonally so the pan tilts and drains gradually rather than dumping all at once.
Once the flow slows, support the pan with one hand while removing the last few bolts. Lower it carefully — there's about a quart of fluid still in the pan.

Remove the filter (one or two bolts depending on year). The filter has an O-ring on the pickup — make sure it comes out with the filter and isn't stuck in the transmission. Losing the O-ring inside the trans is the most common mistake on this job.
Install the new filter with its new O-ring. Don't reuse the old O-ring even if it looks fine.
Clean the pan thoroughly. Wipe out the magnet — fine metal paste is normal, big chunks are bad news. Scrape off any old gasket material.

Install the new pan gasket. Most ATP and Hayden kits come with a reusable rubber gasket — no RTV needed if the kit includes a gasket. If reusing the pan with no gasket, run a 1/8" bead of high-temp RTV.
Reinstall the pan. Torque pan bolts to 13 ft-lbs in a criss-cross pattern. Don't over-torque — the pan flange warps if you crank past 18 ft-lbs.
Lower the vehicle. Add 4.5 quarts of ATF+4 through the dipstick tube using a long-neck funnel or pump.
Start the engine. With your foot on the brake, cycle through every gear position (P-R-N-D-3-2-1, hold each gear for 3 seconds). Return to Park.
Check the dipstick with the engine running and the trans at idle. Cold reading should be between the "Add" and the lower hash mark. Top off to the cold-fill line.
Drive 10 miles. Re-check the level at full operating temp with the engine running, in Park, on a level surface. Top off to the hot full mark.
Check the pan for leaks after the first drive and again 24 hours later.
pros: Cheap insurance for an aging transmission — clutches and bands last longer with clean fluid
Catches metal contamination on the pan magnet before it grinds through the planetary gears
A burnt-smelling drop tells you exactly what state the trans is in before you trail it
cons: Pan-drop service only refreshes ~30% of total fluid — for a true flush you need a shop machine
Aged ZJs with never-serviced fluid can react badly to fresh ATF — old varnish breaks loose and clogs valves
The 42RE/46RE doesn't have a drain plug, so the job is messier than a modern transmission
Over-torquing pan bolts warps the flange — this is the most common DIY mistake

title: Differential Fluid — Dana 30 / Chrysler 8.25 / Dana 44a
tools_required: 13mm socket (cover bolts on most ZJ axles)

parts.name: Gear oil 75W-90 (conventional or synthetic)
parts.part_number: Valvoline VV832 / Mobil 1 75W-90 / Royal Purple Max-Gear

citations.title: ExtremeTerrain — Grand Cherokee ZJ Fluid Capacities
Cherokee Forum — ZJ axle fluid service

summary: Front Dana 30 takes 1.25 quarts. Rear Chrysler 8.25 takes 2.1 quarts. Rear Dana 44a (5.9 Limited and V8 tow package) takes 2.6 quarts. All three want 75W-90 gear oil, and if your rear is Trac-Lok limited-slip you need 4 oz of friction modifier on top.
description:
This is one of the highest-payoff maintenance jobs on a used ZJ — most of them come with whatever fluid was in there when the previous owner stopped caring. Plan on 90 minutes for both axles your first time, half that on the second pass. The cover-off method (no drain plug on these axles) means you'll wipe out old fluid, scrape off the cover, and re-seal with RTV.

Figuring out which rear axle you have: pull the tag on a cover bolt. "8.25" is the Chrysler 8.25 (most 4.0L ZJs). "44" is the Dana 44a (most 5.2/5.9 Magnum ZJs and V8 trailer-tow packages). The Dana 30 is up front on every ZJ — no Dana 44 up front from the factory. The Dana 44a (the "a" is for aluminum center) is lighter than a full Dana 44 but uses the same ring and pinion, so service is the same.

Service interval: every 30,000 miles for street driving. Every 15,000 miles if you wheel, ford water above the diff, or tow regularly. Water intrusion turns gear oil milky — if you pull a cover and see chocolate milk, change it now and check for axle seal damage.
steps: Drive 10–15 minutes first so the gear oil is warm and flows out cleanly. Park on a level surface.
Loosen the lug nuts a quarter turn (wheels still on the ground), then jack and support the vehicle on jack stands. Both axles need to come off the ground so fluid drains evenly.
Position a wide, low drain pan under the diff cover.
Remove all but two of the top cover bolts (13mm on most ZJ axles). Leave one bolt at each upper corner snug — these hold the cover while you crack the seal.
Tap the cover gently with a rubber mallet to break the gasket. Fluid will start running out the bottom.
Once the flow slows, remove the two remaining bolts and pull the cover off. Catch the last cupful of fluid with a rag.
Scrape the old gasket or RTV off both the cover and the axle housing. A razor blade and brake cleaner finish the job. The mating surfaces need to be dry, clean, and oil-free.
Inspect the ring gear and the magnet inside the cover (if present). A small amount of fine metal paste on the magnet is normal. Big chunks of metal mean stop and call a shop.
Apply a 1/4" continuous bead of Ultra Black RTV around the cover, circling the bolt holes on the inside. Let it skin for 5 minutes per the Permatex instructions.
Bolt the cover back on. Torque cover bolts to 30 ft-lbs in a criss-cross pattern. Don't over-torque — stripped cover threads in cast aluminum (the 44a) are a real possibility.
Refill through the fill plug (3/8" square drive on the side of the axle housing). Fill until fluid barely weeps out of the fill hole.
Reinstall the fill plug. Torque to 25 ft-lbs.
Repeat for the second axle.
Drive the vehicle 10 miles, then re-check for leaks at the cover and fill plug. Re-torque cover bolts if needed after a heat cycle.
pros: Cheap insurance — a $30 fluid change extends ring-and-pinion life by 50,000+ miles
Catches problems early: water intrusion, broken teeth, axle seal failure
A clean cover gives you a baseline for future trail wheeling and water crossings
cons: The cover-off method is messier than a drain plug — the 8.25 and Dana 30 don't have one
Aluminum 44a cover threads strip if you over-torque — slow and careful with the torque wrench
Trac-Lok diffs absolutely need the friction modifier or you'll get chatter on tight turns

title: Oil Change — 4.0L and Magnum V8s
tools_required: jack and jack stands or ramps

parts.name: Engine oil — 10W-30 conventional or full synthetic

citations.title: Mopar oil filter compatibility (5281090AB / MO-090)
ZJ fluid capacities reference

summary: The ZJ takes 6 quarts of 10W-30 (4.0L) or 5 quarts (5.2/5.9L Magnum), and Mopar's MO-090 filter fits every engine option. Plan on 30 minutes if everything cooperates and the previous owner didn't overtighten the drain plug.
description:
The ZJ's 4.0L and Magnum V8s are old, low-stress engines that don't care which name brand of oil you run — they care that you run *some* clean oil and change it on time. Use a conventional 10W-30 for high-mileage rigs that already leak; jump to a full synthetic 5W-30 if you live in Phoenix or anywhere else where the engine bakes after shutdown. Skip the heavy 20W-50 unless you're in the middle of summer and watching pressure drop at idle on a tired motor.

Mopar's 5281090AB filter (the box also says MO-090) is the OEM unit and fits the 4.0L, 5.2L Magnum, and 5.9L Magnum — one part number across the whole engine lineup. Wix 51515, Purolator L25288, and Fram TG3614 are the common equivalents. Avoid the smallest Frams; a slightly oversized filter holds more oil and is more manageable to grip when it's hot.

Park on a level surface, run the engine for two minutes to warm and thin the oil, then shut it down. Pull the dipstick to break the vacuum (oil drains faster), set the pan, and crack the drain plug with a 13mm socket. The plug is a tapered design that doesn't need a crush washer, but if yours has been overtightened in the past and weeps, replace it with a Dorman 095-002 plug-and-gasket combo.
steps: Warm the engine for 2 minutes, then shut down. Set the parking brake and chock the rear wheels.
Raise the front of the vehicle on jack stands or drive onto ramps. Working flat on the ground is possible but miserable.
Position the drain pan, remove the dipstick, and loosen the drain plug with a 13mm socket. Let it drain for at least 5 minutes — longer if you have time.
Move the pan under the oil filter (passenger side, near the bottom of the block). Loosen with a filter wrench, then spin off by hand. Watch for the gasket — it should come off with the filter.
Wipe the filter mounting surface clean. Smear fresh oil on the new filter's gasket, then spin the filter on by hand until it contacts the mounting surface, then 3/4 turn more.
Reinstall the drain plug. Torque to 25 ft-lbs. Don't gorilla it — the oil pan is thin steel and the threads strip.
Add 6 quarts (4.0L) or 5 quarts (5.2/5.9L) of fresh oil. Start the engine, watch the pressure light go out within 5 seconds, then shut down.
Wait 5 minutes for the oil to settle, then check the dipstick. Top off to the full mark.
Recycle the old oil — every AutoZone and O'Reilly takes used oil free.
pros: Cheapest maintenance job on the vehicle, and the one that does the most for longevity
The Magnum V8s and the 4.0L share the same filter — one part to stock
Good filter access compared to most modern vehicles (no skid plate to drop, no fender liner to peel)
cons: The drain plug is at the lowest point of a thin steel pan — over-torque it once and you're tapping threads or replacing the pan
The oil filter dumps oil down the frame rail when you spin it off — pre-position cardboard or wipe up after
Magnums burn a little oil between changes by 150K — check the dipstick monthly, not at oil-change time

title: Spark Plugs — 4.0L and 5.2/5.9 Magnum

citations.title: Champion RC12LYC fits 4.0L and Magnum V8 ZJs
ZJ spark plug specs reference

summary: All three ZJ engines run the Champion RC12LYC (or NGK ZFR5N), gapped at 0.035". The 4.0L is a 15-minute job; the Magnum V8s take an hour because the rear plugs hide behind the exhaust manifolds.
description:
The ZJ is one of the rare vehicles where every factory engine option runs the same spark plug. Champion's RC12LYC is the OEM unit — Mopar boxes it as part number 56027275. Gap them to 0.035" before installation, even brand-new in the box; plug gaps drift in shipping and a tight gap will make the 4.0L stumble on cold mornings.

NGK ZFR5N is the equivalent if you can't find Champions. Skip the platinum and iridium upgrades — these engines were designed for copper-electrode plugs, and the high-energy plugs don't last meaningfully longer in a low-compression motor like the 4.0L. Spend the money you save on a real coil pack and cap-and-rotor kit.

On the 4.0L straight-six, all six plugs are on the passenger side of the head, fully accessible from above. Pop the wires off one at a time (don't pull all six and try to remember the firing order — pull, swap, replace, move on). On the Magnum V8s, the front three plugs on each side come out from above; the rear plugs require either a long extension and patience, or removing a wheel and going through the wheel well. Both Magnum approaches work — the wheel-well route is faster after you've done it once.

Anti-seize on the threads is mandatory on the iron heads of the 4.0L — without it, you'll pull aluminum thread material out of the head on the next change. The Magnum V8s also have iron heads; anti-seize is still recommended. Use a light coat — too much and you'll over-torque the plug because the friction is misleading.
steps: Let the engine cool fully. Pulling plugs from a warm aluminum-headed engine pulls threads; the ZJ has iron heads but the rule still applies — cold is better.
Number the spark plug wires with masking tape (1-2-3-4-5-6 on the I6, 1-3-5-7 driver side and 2-4-6-8 passenger on the V8s). This saves you if the firing order on the cap is unclear.
Working one cylinder at a time: pull the wire from the plug by gripping the boot (not the wire), then remove the plug with the 5/8" spark plug socket.
Gap the new plug to 0.035" using a wire-style gap tool. Check every plug — don't trust the factory gap.
Apply a thin coat of anti-seize to the plug threads (the threads, not the electrode).
Hand-thread the new plug into the head — if it doesn't spin in easily by hand, back it out and try again. Cross-threading the head is a $300 mistake.
Torque the plug. 4.0L: 27 ft-lbs. Magnum V8s: 30 ft-lbs.
Apply a small dab of dielectric grease to the inside of the wire boot, then reinstall the wire. You should feel and hear it click onto the plug.
Repeat for each cylinder. Start the engine and listen for a smooth idle — if it stumbles, you missed a wire.
pros: All three ZJ engines share the same plug — one set in your spares kit covers the whole platform
Champion RC12LYC is under $4 a plug — cheapest scheduled-maintenance item on the truck
Fresh plugs noticeably wake up a tired Magnum V8 and steady out the 4.0L's idle
cons: The rear plugs on the Magnum V8s are buried behind the exhaust manifolds — patience required
Iron heads are forgiving but cross-threading still happens — always hand-start every plug
Skip the platinum/iridium upgrade hype — these engines don't benefit from it

title: Transfer Case Fluid — NP242 and NP249
tools_required: 3/8" ratchet (no socket — the plug has a square drive head)
fluid pump (hand pump or squeeze bottle with hose)

citations.title: ZJ NP242/NP249 fluid capacity and procedure
NP242 fluid change reference

summary: Both the NP242 (Selec-Trac) and NP249 (Quadra-Trac) in the ZJ take ATF. The NP242 holds 1.4 quarts; the NP249 holds 1.25 quarts. Buy 2 quarts of any name-brand ATF and you've got the job covered. Plan on 30 minutes.
description:
The ZJ shipped with one of three transfer cases: the NP231 (rare, manual transmission only), the NP242 Selec-Trac (the part-time/full-time selectable case that most ZJs got), and the NP249 Quadra-Trac (full-time with a viscous coupling — found mostly on the Limited and Orvis trims). All three take ATF, not gear oil. Running gear oil in any of them will destroy the viscous coupling (NP249) or the planetary gears (NP242). Don't experiment.

ATF type doesn't matter much — the original Mopar spec was Dexron II, but ATF+4 works fine and is what's on the parts store shelf today. Valvoline MaxLife is a popular budget choice and has run trouble-free in thousands of ZJs. The NP249 with a worn viscous coupling will shudder in tight turns at low speed regardless of fluid — that's a coupling failure, not a fluid problem.

The fill and drain plugs are both 3/8" square drive — no socket needed. Stick your 3/8" ratchet directly into the plug. Crack the fill plug first, before you drain — if the fill plug is seized, you don't want to find out after you've emptied the case. Some old fill plugs round off; have a pair of vice grips on standby.
steps: Drive the vehicle for 10 minutes to warm the fluid. Warm fluid drains faster and carries out more contamination.
Park on a level surface, set the parking brake, chock the wheels. Raise the rear of the vehicle (you can do this with both rear wheels on jack stands, or with the whole vehicle on a lift).
Locate the transfer case behind the transmission. The fill plug is on the upper rear; the drain plug is on the lower rear.
Crack the fill plug first. If it spins out, you're clear to drain. Reinstall it loosely.
Position the drain pan under the drain plug. Remove the drain plug. Let it drain fully — usually 3–5 minutes.
Inspect the magnetic drain plug (NP242 has one, NP249 does not). A light film of metallic dust is normal; chunks or shavings mean internal damage and a fluid change won't fix it.
Wipe the drain plug clean, reinstall, torque to 25 ft-lbs.
Remove the fill plug. Pump fresh ATF into the case until fluid runs out the fill hole (not down — out, level). NP242: about 1.4 quarts. NP249: about 1.25 quarts.
Reinstall the fill plug, torque to 25 ft-lbs.
Lower the vehicle. Take it for a short drive and re-check for leaks at both plugs.
pros: Cheapest drivetrain service on the ZJ — under $20 in fluid
The magnetic drain plug on the NP242 gives you a free condition report each time you service the case
Fresh ATF restores smooth shifting between 2H/4H/4L modes on the NP242
cons: Both fill and drain plugs use a 3/8" square drive head that rounds off easily on old, dry cases — bring vice grips
NP249 shudder in tight turns at low speed is a viscous coupling failure, not fixable with new fluid — it's a transfer case rebuild or a swap to NP242
Overfilling pushes fluid out the vent and onto your exhaust — fill level is "until it runs out the fill hole," not "as much as the spec card says"

title: Winch and Mount for the ZJ

citations.title: cad4x4 — Jeep Grand Cherokee ZJ winch plate with skid plate
JCR Offroad — DIY ZJ winch bumper

summary: A winch is the difference between an embarrassing wait for a strap and getting yourself out, but on a unibody ZJ the mount matters as much as the winch. A pull rated higher than the structure it bolts to will fold sheet metal before it moves the truck, so the winch and its mounting plate are one decision, not two.
description:
Rate the winch around 1.5 times the loaded weight of the ZJ — a built six-cylinder ZJ on 32s lands around 8,000 to 9,500 pounds of capacity. Synthetic line is the better choice for a trail rig: lighter, safer when it fails, and kinder to handle than wire rope. Spring for a quality solenoid pack; the winch is a safety tool and the cheapest units fail when you need them.

The ZJ has no factory frame horns to hang a winch on, so a dedicated winch plate or winch bumper that ties into the frame rails and unibody is required. The cad4x4 and JCR designs in the sources combine a winch plate with a skid so the mount also protects the underbody. Do not bolt a winch to a bumper bracket meant only to hold a bumper.

The winch draws enormous current, so run correctly sized cable straight to the battery with an inline disconnect or breaker. Keep the runs short, the connections clean and protected, and consider the charging and battery upgrade that heavy winching wants — a long pull can flatten a stock battery and stress the alternator.

Treat the winch and its mount as one purchase. Rate the winch to roughly 1.5 times the loaded truck, run synthetic line, and mount it to a plate or bumper that ties into the frame. Then wire it with cable sized for the draw and a disconnect close to the battery. A winch is a safety tool, so buy quality once.

title: Track Bar Replacement and Upgrade

parts.name: Heavy-duty adjustable track bar (Core 4x4 Cruise Series)
Kevin's Offroad Hard-KOR track bar conversion

citations.title: Kevin's Offroad — Death Wobble cures and ZJ track bar conversions
Core 4x4 — ZJ Cruise Series adjustable track bar

summary: The front track bar holds the axle laterally centered under the truck. A worn track bar lets the axle dance side to side over bumps, and on a coil-sprung four-link like the ZJ that's a primary cause of death wobble. Replace the bar before chasing anything else if the steering wheel oscillates at speed.
description:
The ZJ front track bar is one of the weakest links in the steering system. The bushing at the frame end fails (sometimes you can see daylight through the bushing eye), and the threaded upper rod end develops play. Both ends contribute to lateral axle slop. Even on a perfectly aligned, stock-height ZJ, a worn track bar will produce wandering steering and feel like a soft tie rod.

Two upgrade paths. Stock-replacement bars (Moog DS1417, Mopar OE) get you back to factory tightness for under $100 — the right call for daily-driven, stock-height ZJs. Adjustable heavy-duty bars (Core 4x4 Cruise Series, Kevin's Offroad Hard-KOR) use DOM tubing, a Johnny Joint or heim at the adjustable end, and a polyurethane or solid bushing at the fixed end. They tighten the front end noticeably and recenter the axle if you've lifted the truck. Plan on $250–$300 for a real heavy-duty kit.

Frame bracket warning: the factory track bar bracket on the frame is stamped steel and bends over time, especially on lifted ZJs. If the frame end of the bar tracks visibly bent, you need a reinforced bracket (StinkyFab and Iron Rock both make them) — installing a heavy-duty track bar onto a bent factory bracket lasts about six months.

Death wobble note. The track bar is one of five components to inspect if you have death wobble. The other four: ball joints, tie rod ends, steering box (sector shaft play), and unit bearings. Replacing the track bar alone solves death wobble maybe 40% of the time. Combine it with ball joint and tie rod checks for an 80–95% cure rate. See the related ZJ death wobble guide.

Service interval: inspect at every oil change. Replace when the bushing tears or when the threaded end has visible play.
steps: Loosen the front lug nuts a quarter turn. Jack the front of the vehicle and support the frame on jack stands. Both front wheels off the ground.
Remove the front wheels for working access (optional but recommended).
Soak both track bar bolts with PB Blaster. Let it work for 10 minutes.

Remove the axle-end bolt (21mm). The axle end is typically a tapered stud that needs a tie rod puller or sharp hammer blow on the bracket to break free. Don't beat directly on the stud — you'll mushroom it.
Remove the frame-end bolt (18mm). The bushing end is a straight-through bolt.
Lift the old track bar out. Compare the new bar's length on the bench to make sure you have the right part.
Install the new bar. If it's adjustable, set the length so the front axle sits centered under the truck — measure from a fixed frame point to each tire sidewall and adjust until both sides match.
Bolt the new track bar in hand-tight at both ends.
Lower the vehicle so it sits on its own weight on the ground.

With the truck at ride height, torque both bolts to 74 ft-lbs (FSM spec for the 1993-1998 ZJ — verify in your service manual). Torquing at ride height (not at full droop) is mandatory so the bushing isn't preloaded.
Re-check axle centering by measuring frame-to-tire on both sides. If off, adjust an adjustable bar; on a stock bar, slight off-center is unavoidable and the alignment shop will compensate.
Drive 20 miles. Re-check torque on both ends.
Schedule an alignment within 200 miles — track bar replacement shifts caster slightly.
pros: Single biggest steering improvement on a tired ZJ for the dollar
One of the five core components in any death-wobble diagnosis
Adjustable bars let you recenter the axle on lifted trucks — required above 2.5" of lift
cons: A new track bar alone won't fix death wobble if the ball joints, tie rods, or steering box are also worn
Beating on the axle-end stud with a hammer damages the threads — use a tie rod puller or a careful side-blow on the bracket
Skipping the torque-at-ride-height step preloads the bushing and shortens its life
Alignment is needed after — budget another $100–$150 at a shop

title: Death Wobble Diagnosis

citations.title: Jeep Grand Cherokee ZJ reference
Iron Rock Off Road ZJ steering

summary: The ZJ has a coil-sprung solid front axle located by a track bar — the exact layout that produces classic death wobble when a joint wears. The violent shake after hitting a bump at speed is a symptom, never the disease. The disease is play in the track bar, tie-rod ends, or ball joints, and you find it before you drive the truck again.
description:
Death wobble is a safety issue, full stop — if it has started, take the ZJ off the highway until it is fixed. The mechanism is a feedback loop: a worn locating joint lets the axle shimmy, the shimmy feeds itself through the steering, and only slowing to a near-stop breaks it. The single most common culprit on the ZJ is the track bar — both its ends and its mounting holes, which elongate. Grab the bar and try to move it; any play at either end or at the frame bracket means replace it.

Work the rest of the front end methodically with the wheels off the ground. Check tie-rod ends and the drag link for play, check ball joints at 12-and-6, and confirm the control-arm bushings are not cracked or collapsed. Loose wheel bearings and an out-of-balance tire can trigger or worsen wobble, so include those. Re-torque the track bar and control-arm bolts to spec — a loose factory bolt mimics a worn part.

Do not chase death wobble with a bigger steering stabilizer. A stabilizer masks the onset and convinces owners the truck is fixed while the worn joint keeps degrading. Replace what is worn, torque everything correctly, and the stabilizer becomes what it should be: a refinement, not a band-aid.
steps: Stop driving the ZJ at highway speed until diagnosis is complete.
With the front lifted, check the track bar ends and frame bracket for any play first.
Inspect tie-rod ends, drag link, ball joints, and control-arm bushings.
Re-torque track bar and control-arm bolts to factory spec; check wheel bearings and tire balance.
Replace worn parts, then road-test at increasing speed in a safe area.

title: Control Arm and Bushing Replacement
tools_required: bushing press or shop press (if reusing arms with new bushings)
rotary tool or hacksaw (cutting out stuck bushings)
skills_required: bushing pressing or replacing complete arms

parts.name: Energy Suspension polyurethane bushing kit (full set)

citations.title: Quadratec — ZJ control arm bushings catalog
JeepForum — ZJ front lower control arm bushing replacement

summary: Both ZJ axles use a four-link with rubber-bushed control arms. After 25 years the bushings are torn, sloppy, or missing chunks — they steer the truck around like a drunk pendulum. Replace complete arms instead of pressing in new bushings unless you own a shop press. The labor difference makes new arms the better deal for most owners.
description:
Three failure modes give themselves away. A clunk on takeoff after parking on a slope is a torn lower control arm bushing on the front. Wandering steering on highway at speed is upper control arm bushing play. A "click-click-click" over expansion joints in cold weather is the rear lower control arm bushing. Get under the truck with a pry bar and lever each arm at the axle end — if you can move it noticeably, the bushing is gone.

Buying decisions. Complete replacement arms with bushings pre-pressed run $50–$80 per arm in Moog or Mevotech. Pressing new bushings into your existing arms saves money but requires a shop press, a bushing driver set, and patience for the stuck ones — figure 2–3 hours per arm versus 45 minutes for a complete-arm swap. The complete arm is the better deal unless you already have the press.

Polyurethane bushings (Energy Suspension 2.3104G) last longer and tighten up the truck's handling at the cost of more noise transmission and faster wear at the ball joint end. Rubber is fine for daily drivers. Poly is the right call if you've already accepted the squeak in trade for tight steering.

Pinion angle warning: if you've lifted the ZJ above 2.5", stock-length control arms will pull the pinion up at the front and down at the rear. Adjustable arms (Iron Rock, Currie, JKS) fix this. Stock arms with stock geometry are correct on stock-height ZJs.
steps: Loosen the lug nuts a quarter turn. Jack the front of the vehicle and support the frame on jack stands. Both wheels off the ground.
Remove the front wheels.
