Support the front axle with a floor jack so it doesn't drop when the lower arm comes free.
Soak the lower arm bolts with PB Blaster. Let it work for 15 minutes.
Remove the front lower control arm bolt at the axle end (21mm). It may need a breaker bar — the bolt sees a lot of stress.
Remove the front lower control arm bolt at the frame end (21mm).
Lift the arm out. If a bushing is stuck on a bolt sleeve, use a long pry bar to walk it off.
Install the new arm with new hardware (the kits include new bolts and nuts — use them; the old bolts are weakened from corrosion). Torque hand-tight only for now.
Repeat steps 5–8 for the front upper arm. The upper arm bolts are tighter to reach — a swivel socket on a long extension is the trick.
Repeat for the opposite side. Then move to the rear axle.
Rear lower arms (21mm at axle, 21mm at frame). Same procedure — support the axle, remove old, install new.
Rear upper arms (21mm at axle, 18mm at frame on most years).
Lower the vehicle so it sits on its own weight on the ground.
Torque all four lower arm bolts to 100 ft-lbs. Torque all four upper arm bolts to 75 ft-lbs. (Verify in the FSM for your year — some V8 ZJs spec slightly different values.)
Drive 20 miles and re-check all torque values. Bushings settle in the first few hundred miles.
pros: Restores steering precision — a ZJ with all 8 arms fresh feels 10 years younger
Most ZJs on the road today have at least 2 arms with torn bushings — fixing them is the single biggest handling upgrade
Complete-arm replacement is straightforward DIY work with hand tools
cons: Pressing bushings into the original arms requires a shop press and a lot of patience
Polyurethane bushings squeak in cold weather — many owners regret them on daily drivers
The upper arm frame bolts are in a tight space; expect skinned knuckles
Torque at ride height is mandatory or the bushing preloads and tears early

title: Quadra-Coil Rear Suspension Service
tools_required: second floor jack or pole jack (to support axle)

parts.name: Sway bar end links (pair, if rotted)

citations.title: Cherokee Forum — ZJ/WJ coil spring replacement how-to
Quadratec — ZJ coil springs catalog

summary: ZJ Quadra-Coil rear is a four-link with coil springs — same architecture as the XJ and TJ rear, with two lower arms, two uppers, a track bar, and a coil over each spring perch. Service is straightforward once you know to support the axle before you unbolt anything.
description:
The Quadra-Coil name was Chrysler's marketing for "coil springs front and rear" — there is no air, no electronic damping, no exotic geometry. Front and rear are both solid-axle coil-sprung four-link setups. That's part of why the ZJ runs circles around the later WK on a trail: it's a genuinely capable platform with straightforward suspension. Stock coils sag after 25 years and will let the bump stops touch the axle tube on a hard compression. Stock shocks are toast on any ZJ that hasn't seen new ones in the last decade.

Decisions before you order parts. If the ZJ rides like a brick and sits low in the rear, replace coils and shocks together. If it rides okay but bottoms out over speed bumps, do shocks. Bilstein 5100 is the gold-standard street/light-trail shock for a stock-height ZJ. Rancho RS5000X is the budget pick. Monroe and KYB white-box shocks are economy options — they work but won't outlast Bilsteins.

Lift options: A 2" lift spring upgrade is the sweet spot for 31" tires. Iron Rock Off Road, Old Man Emu, and Rusty's all make ZJ-specific 2" lift coils. Anything taller than 3" on a ZJ requires adjustable control arms and a longer track bar — see the related control arm guide.

Service interval: shocks every 60,000–80,000 miles, springs only when sagging or damaged. Inspect upper coil isolators every shock change — they crumble and let the spring contact bare metal.
steps: Loosen the rear lug nuts a quarter turn. Jack the rear of the vehicle and support the frame on jack stands forward of the lower control arm mounts.
Remove the wheels.
Place a second floor jack under the axle differential housing, snug but not lifting.
Disconnect the rear sway bar end links (15mm). If they're rotted, replace them rather than fight to save them.
Remove the lower shock bolt (18mm) on each side. Pull the shocks free at the bottom and let them hang on the upper mount.
Disconnect the rear track bar at the axle (21mm). This lets the axle drop straight down rather than swing sideways.
Slowly lower the floor jack under the axle. The coil springs will extend and eventually unseat. Stop when the springs are loose — usually 4–6" of axle drop.
Remove the coil springs by hand. They lift right out once unloaded.
Inspect the upper coil isolators in the frame pocket. Replace if cracked or crumbling.
Set the new coil springs in the lower spring perch and align them in the upper isolator pocket. Make sure the coil end seats in the locator notch in the lower perch.
Raise the axle back up with the floor jack. The springs should compress into place as the axle rises.
Reconnect the track bar (21mm) but don't fully torque yet. Reconnect the sway bar end links.
Install new shocks: lower bolt 23 ft-lbs, upper nut 23 ft-lbs (typical — verify in service manual for your year).
Lower the vehicle so it sits on its own weight, then torque the track bar bolt to 74 ft-lbs. Torquing at ride height (not droop) is what keeps the bushing from preloading.
Re-torque all suspension bolts to spec.
Drive 20 miles and re-check all fasteners.
pros: Restores correct ride height — a sagged ZJ rear changes pinion angle and stresses the slip yoke
New shocks transform the truck's road manners — old gas-charged ZJ shocks lose damping by 80,000 miles
A genuinely DIY-friendly Quadra-Coil rear — no spring compressors needed if you support the axle
cons: Failure to torque the track bar at ride height preloads the bushing and you'll feel it through the steering on every bump
Upper coil isolators are cheap but straightforward to forget — replace them while you're in there
Lift coils plus stock control arms = ugly pinion angle; budget for adjustable arms above 2.5"

title: Shock Upgrade for a Lifted ZJ

citations.title: Iron Rock Off Road — ZJ 93-98 suspension
Rocky Road Outfitters — ZJ OME lift and shocks

summary: The single most common ZJ suspension mistake is bolting on a lift and reusing tired, too-short factory shocks. A coil-sprung ZJ rides and flexes only as well as its dampers allow, so the shock is not an afterthought — it is the part that decides whether your lift works.
description:
The ZJ uses coil springs at all four corners (Quadra-Coil), so the shock does not hold the truck up — it controls how the axle moves. Add three or four inches of lift and a stock-length shock tops out early in droop, which limits articulation and slams the suspension into its own internal stop. Pick a shock valved and lengthed for your lift: roughly a 3-inch lift wants a shock about 2 inches longer extended than stock, and a 4.5-inch kit wants more again. Confirm the collapsed length still clears the bump stop at full compression.

A firmer monotube like a Bilstein 5100 suits a ZJ that sees pavement and graded forest road and wants body control at speed. A softer twin-tube such as an Old Man Emu rides plush and flexes well at crawling speed. Neither is wrong — match the valving to where the truck actually spends its time.

Replace shocks in pairs, axle by axle, with the suspension supported. Soak the upper studs in penetrant before turning them; a rusted ZJ shock stud will snap and turn a one-hour job into a drill-and-tap afternoon. Torque to spec and recheck after the first trail run. If your lift puts the shock at the end of its travel, add the correct relocation bracket rather than running it bottomed out.

On a coil-sprung ZJ the shock is not a consumable to ignore — it sets ride quality, articulation, and how hard the suspension slams its stops. Buy the right length for your lift, valve it for where you actually drive, and replace both ends in pairs. It is the cheapest part of a lift that makes the biggest difference to how the truck feels.

title: Lift Kit Guide

citations.title: Iron Rock Off Road ZJ suspension
Quadratec ZJ suspension catalog

summary: The ZJ is coil-sprung at all four corners (Quadra-Coil), so a lift is coil springs and longer shocks, not spring packs. A 3–4 inch kit clears 31–32" tires and is the sweet spot; past that the unibody and short wheelbase fight you, and the work grows faster than the payoff.
description:
Verdict: a quality 3–4" coil kit with an adjustable front track bar is the right ZJ build for a capable trail rig on 31–32s. The ZJ's Achilles' heel under a lift is geometry — raising a coil, track-bar-located front axle without correcting the track bar pulls the axle off-center and steepens the control-arm angles, which is exactly what triggers death wobble. An adjustable track bar is not optional above 3 inches; it is the part that keeps the steering safe.

Budget for the supporting cast. Extended brake lines clear the added droop, sway-bar disconnects let the front axle flex (the ZJ's short arms otherwise bind), and longer shocks matched to the lift keep you off the bump stops. On V8 trucks watch the front driveshaft angle; on the 4.0L, the rear pinion angle wants a shim above ~3.5 inches to stop vibration.

Keep your tire goal honest. 31s transform the ZJ with almost no drama. 32s need the full 4" and trimming. 33s on a ZJ mean cutting, a rear axle that can take it (see the Dana 35 vs 44 guide), and accepting that the short wheelbase gets twitchy — it is a build, not a bolt-on.
steps: Lift, support the unibody, and unload the coils one corner at a time.
Install coils and matched shocks; do not reuse tired stock shocks.
Fit an adjustable front track bar and re-center the axle under the body.
Add extended brake lines and sway-bar disconnects; set rear pinion angle above 3.5 in.
Alignment afterward — set caster back into range or the steering will wander.

title: Diagnosing the ZJ — OBD1 (1993–1995) vs OBD2 (1996–1998)
tools_required: scan tool (OBD2) or no tool (OBD1 flash codes)

citations.title: ZJ OBD1 Flash Code Procedure — ZJ Grand Cherokee Tech
Chrysler OBD2 Code Reference — AllPar.com

summary: The ZJ spans the OBD1-to-OBD2 transition — 1993–1995 models use Chrysler's pre-OBD2 flash code system, while 1996–1998 use the standardized OBD2 port. Knowing which system you have determines which diagnostic approach to use.
description:
The split is simple by model year: **1993, 1994, and 1995 ZJs are OBD1**. **1996, 1997, and 1998 ZJs are OBD2**. There is no ambiguity by production date — it is strictly the model year.

On the 1996–1998 ZJ, the OBD2 port is a standard 16-pin trapezoid connector located under the dashboard on the driver's side. Any OBD2 scanner — including the $30 Bluetooth adapters that pair with phone apps — will communicate with this port. Chrysler's OBD2 implementation is fully standard; you do not need a dealer-specific tool.

The 1993–1995 ZJ has no OBD2 port. It uses the Chrysler OBDI system, which stores codes in the PCM and outputs them as blink codes via the check engine light.

The procedure is simple and requires no tools:

1. Turn the ignition key to **ON-OFF-ON-OFF-ON** within 5 seconds. The key should not go to START — stop at ON each time.
2. Watch the check engine light. It will begin flashing a sequence of two-digit codes.
3. Count the flashes: the light will flash once (pause), then a number of times equal to the first digit, then pause, then flash the second digit. For example, Code 23 = one flash, pause, then two flashes, longer pause, then three flashes.
4. After all codes have flashed, the sequence ends with Code 55 — this is the "end of codes" signal.
5. Write down every code before 55.

Code 55 by itself (with no other codes) means the system is clean. The flash code system on the 1993–1995 ZJ covers the major sensors — TPS, MAP, coolant temp, O2 sensor, CPS, and ignition. It will not cover every possible fault, but the most common failure modes (like the crankshaft position sensor) have assigned codes.

**P0340 / P0344 (OBD2) or Code 21 (OBD1):** Crankshaft position sensor circuit — the most common ZJ 4.0L fault code. Replace the CPS as described in the engine guide.

**P0300 (OBD2):** Random/multiple cylinder misfire. Check spark plugs, plug wires, and fuel pressure before assuming an internal engine issue.

**P1389 / P1388 (OBD2) or Code 42 (OBD1):** Auto Shutdown (ASD) relay or fuel pump relay circuit. The ASD relay controls the fuel pump, ignition coil, and injectors. A failing ASD relay causes intermittent stall and no-start conditions.

**P0128 (OBD2):** Coolant temperature below threshold — thermostat stuck open. Replace the thermostat.

**P0420 (OBD2):** Catalyst efficiency below threshold — O2 sensor or catalytic converter issue. Common on higher-mileage ZJs.

**Code 13 / P0108 (MAP sensor circuit):** Manifold absolute pressure sensor high voltage. Clean the MAP sensor connector and test the sensor; the ZJ MAP sensor is on the intake manifold and is prone to connector corrosion.

For deeper OBD1 diagnosis beyond flash codes — reading live data like coolant temperature, O2 sensor voltage, and fuel trims — the factory Chrysler DRB III scan tool is the proper tool. These are expensive and dealer-specific. The Actron CP9145 is the most widely-used aftermarket OBD1 Chrysler scanner and reads codes, clears codes, and displays a subset of live data. At around $65–70 used, it is the practical choice for a ZJ owner who wants more than flash codes.

For OBD2 (1996–1998), any standard scanner works. The Autel AL519 or Actron CP9600 are good entry-level tools. For more serious diagnosis including live data streams, an Autel MX808 or similar mid-tier tool is worth having.

title: Recovery Points on the ZJ Unibody Grand Cherokee

parts.name: Boomerang Automotive ZJ rear recovery mount

citations.title: ZJ Recovery Point Guide — ZJ Grand Cherokee Forum
Unibody Recovery Point Safety — Pirate4x4

summary: The ZJ Grand Cherokee is a unibody — there are no traditional frame rails running front to back. Recovery hardware must attach to the engineered structural points: the front frame horns and the rear subframe crossmember. Using any other attachment point risks ripping out bodywork or injuring bystanders.
description:
On a body-on-frame Jeep — a Wrangler, a CJ — you can weld D-ring tabs to the frame anywhere along its length and trust the frame rail to handle the load. The ZJ unibody does not have continuous frame rails. The front frame horns (the forward extensions of the unibody structure) are the designed front recovery attachment, and the rear subframe crossmember area is the designed rear attachment. Everything else — door sills, bumper fascia, body panels — is not a recovery point.

This matters practically: a zj with a body-colored plastic bumper cover and no reinforced front bumper has no reliable front recovery attachment beyond the factory tow hooks. Confirm what hardware you have before you need a recovery.

The ZJ front frame horns carry the factory tow hooks on most trims. These hooks are adequate for a straight-back pull with a snatch strap — they are the engineered attachment point. Inspect them for rust before relying on them. Frame horns that are lightly surface-rusted are fine; frame horns that are perforated or soft from rust are not trustworthy and must be addressed (see rust-repair-zj).

The better solution for a trail build is an aftermarket steel front bumper with integrated D-ring tabs. Armor Works and Iron Cross both make ZJ-specific bumpers that mount to the front frame horns with additional mounting hardware. These bumpers distribute recovery loads across a larger area of the frame horn structure and provide rated D-ring attachment points. This is the recommended front recovery setup for any ZJ used on technical trails.

D-ring tabs welded to a factory-style steel bumper are significantly stronger than a snatch strap looped through a tow hook. Use 3/4" rated shackles — never use a bolt or makeshift hardware.

The ZJ's rear is served by the trailer hitch receiver, if equipped. The Class III 2" receiver hitch mounts to the rear crossmember of the unibody subframe and is the proper rear recovery attachment. Use a shackle in the receiver (with a hitch pin to retain it) or a receiver-mounted D-ring adapter. Rate the receiver hitch at no more than 50% of its advertised tongue weight for recovery use — the dynamic loads in a snatch strap recovery are significantly higher than a static tow.

For a more robust rear recovery setup, Boomerang Automotive makes a bolt-on rear recovery point kit for the ZJ that mounts to the rear subframe directly and provides two rated D-ring attachment points. This is the right solution if the ZJ does not have a receiver hitch or if you want dedicated recovery hardware separate from the tow hitch.

**The spare tire carrier on the tailgate is never a recovery point.** The tailgate hinges and latch are not designed for recovery loads — a recovery pull from the spare tire carrier risks tearing off the entire tailgate assembly.

title: Tire Sizing — 31s, 32s, and 33s

citations.title: Iron Rock Off Road — ZJ 93-98 suspension and fitment
Rocky Road Outfitters — ZJ lift and tire packages

summary: Tire size is where ZJ builds most often overreach. The truck looks like it can swallow 33s, but the short wheelbase, the unibody, and the rear axle all push back. Pick the size your lift and axle actually support and the ZJ stays a capable, predictable trail rig instead of a rubbing, twitchy compromise.
description:
On a stock-to-mild ZJ, a 31-inch all-terrain bolts on with at most minor trimming and transforms grip with almost no drama. A 32 needs the full 3 to 4 inches of lift and some fender and pinch-seam trimming. A 33 means a 4.5-inch lift, real cutting, a rear axle that can take the load, and accepting that the short wheelbase gets nervous at speed. Bigger than 33 on a ZJ is a fabrication project, not a fitment.

Tire width is nothing without the right wheel offset. A wheel with too much backspacing rubs the control arms and steering at lock; too little pushes the tire into the flare and loads the wheel bearings. A 15x8 or 16x8 with roughly 3.75 to 4.25 inches of backspacing is the common ZJ target. Keep the five-tire set matched so your spare actually fits a locked axle.

Bigger tires change everything downstream: they lengthen braking, slow the gearing, and load the steering. Re-gear to recover the ratio, keep the steering and track bar tight to head off death wobble, and air down on the trail to put the bigger footprint to work. Treat the tire as the center of a system, not a standalone purchase.

The ZJ rewards a tire choice that respects its short wheelbase. A 31 is the no-drama sweet spot, a 32 is the most you should run on a daily-driven ZJ, and a 33 commits you to a full lift, trimming, and a stout rear axle. Decide the tire first, then build the lift, gears, and steering to support it.

title: Wheel Selection for the ZJ Grand Cherokee

citations.title: ZJ Wheel and Tire Guide — JeepForum

summary: The ZJ uses the 5x4.5" (5x114.3mm) bolt pattern — the same as the TJ and JK Wrangler — which opens up a wide aftermarket selection. Get the backspacing right and 33s fit cleanly with a 2" lift.
description:
The ZJ Grand Cherokee uses a **5x4.5" (5x114.3mm)** bolt pattern with a 71.5mm center bore. This is the same pattern as the YJ, TJ, and JK Wrangler, which means the enormous wheel selection developed for those platforms carries directly over. Steel wheels designed for TJ trail use work on the ZJ with no modification.

The ZJ uses M14x1.5 lug nuts — standard Chrysler/Jeep hardware. Match lug nuts to the wheel seat type (conical 60-degree seat is standard for aftermarket wheels).

Backspacing is the key measurement for fitment. The ZJ's factory backspacing varies by trim: approximately 5.25–5.5" on factory 15" steel wheels (which is fairly tucked in). For a trail build running 33x12.5 tires:

**3.75" backspacing on a 15x8" wheel** is the standard recommendation with 2–3" of lift. This pushes the tire out from the factory position and prevents rubbing on the inner fender during full steering lock. With proper trimming of the inner mud flaps, 33s fit this setup well.

Going narrower (under 3.5" backspacing) on a 15x8" wheel pushes the tire too far outside the fender and creates clearance issues at the front bumper and flare edge. Going deeper (over 4.5" backspacing) on a wide tire causes contact on the upper control arm or coil spring perch at full droop.

The ZJ factory wheels are 15" on most trims. A 16x8" wheel with the correct backspacing works well and opens up better tire selection in the 265/75R16 and 285/70R16 range. The 16" market has more trail-oriented tire options than 15". Either size works; choose based on tire selection preference.

For a dedicated trail rig, **steel wheels** are the practical choice. A 15x8" steel wheel runs $60–80 per corner; they dent rather than crack on rock impacts, they can be straightened with heat if badly bent, and a damaged one is cheap to replace. Black Rock, Mopar Trail, and Pro Comp all make straightforward steel trail wheels in 5x4.5".

Alloy wheels look better and save a few pounds per corner. The Method 305 NV and Black Rhino Armory are trail-focused alloys with thick lips and aggressive styling. At $185–200 each they are a significant cost increase, and a cracked alloy on a remote trail is a more serious problem than a bent steel. Choose alloy if the ZJ sees significant street use; choose steel if it spends most of its life on the trail.
